metadata.prompt: A dark, cinematic shot of a person's hand holding a sleek smartphone; the screen is a brilliant, glowing white rectangle.
An SMS message bubble that is physically sharpening into a jagged, red-tipped glass spear.
A close-up of a 'Delivery Alert' text message where the link is a jumble of random letters like bit.ly/3x8f9Z_Fake.
A stylized 3D QR code that is transparent, allowing a digital eye to peer through it into a server room.
A physical poster on a wall where a small, corner-curled QR sticker is being lifted, revealing a red 'SCAM' icon underneath.
A smartphone camera lens focusing on a QR code, with a red 'DANGER' warning appearing on the viewfinder.
A digital maze where the walls are made of mobile phone screens, and a red laser is blocked at every turn.
A giant mechanical padlock snapping shut over the front of a smartphone.
A clean mobile browser interface where the user is typing 'www.bank.com' into the URL bar, ignoring a text notification.

content.narrative: Your mobile device is not just a phone. It is a high-trust, pocket-sized vulnerability. You are accustomed to phishing in your inbox. But now we have Smishing—Phishing via SMS. The data shows that the 'Click Rate' on text messages is significantly higher than email. You feel a sense of person-to-person intimacy on your phone that attackers exploit. And then there is Quishing—Phishing via QR codes. Attackers will paste a fake QR code over a legitimate one at a restaurant or a corporate poster. Your phone’s camera doesn't audit the destination; it just follows the link. On a mobile screen, the URL bar is often hidden or truncated. You can't hover. The protocol for Mobile Signal Recovery: Treat every unsolicited text as a Phish. Never click the link in the message. Open your browser. Type the official address yourself. Don't let your intimacy with the device become your undoing.
content.persona_direction: Rogue AI (The Glitch) - Intrusive, sharp, uncompromising.
content.speaker: Rogue AI

content: Risk: Higher click rates on mobile devices
Mandatory: Never click unsolicited mobile links
Rule: Manually type URLs into your browser

content.question: Why is it more dangerous to click a link on a mobile phone than on a desktop computer?
options: Mobile phones are made of less secure materials.
It is harder to 'hover' and inspect URLs on a small screen.
Desktop computers automatically delete phishing emails.
content.correct_answer: It is harder to 'hover' and inspect URLs on a small screen.
